item.title: Man wanted in robbery tied to Penn State student's murder now sought after off-duty cop shootout
item.description: U.S. Marshals offer a cash reward for Khadfi Fleming, 19, linked to a Penn State student's robbery case and an aggravated assault on a Philly officer.
item.content:encoded:
A 19-year-old wanted in the robbery tied to the killing of a Penn State student is now being sought in connection with another violent Philadelphia crime after an off-duty police officer exchanged gunfire with suspected car thieves.

Khadfi Fleming is a person of interest in the Monday aggravated assault of the off-duty officer, according to the U.S. Marshals Service, which is offering an immediate cash reward for information leading to his whereabouts.

The confrontation unfolded early Monday after thieves allegedly targeted the officer's Dodge Charger, Fox 29 Philadelphia reported.

OFF-DUTY TROOPER AND ARMED CITIZEN HAILED AS HEROES AFTER RETURNING FIRE ON IN-N-OUT GUNMAN

The off-duty officer followed the suspects and confronted them, leading to an exchange of gunfire, according to the outlet. No one is believed to have been struck.

The suspects escaped, and investigators later recovered the officer's Charger with a broken window and damage to its steering column, along with numerous 9mm shell casings, Fox 29 reported.

Authorities say the suspects moved to another stolen car – a Lexus that was later found abandoned.

The U.S. Marshals Service has since publicly identified Fleming as a person of interest in the aggravated assault.

MARSHALS NAB TEEN WANTED FOR MURDER OF PENN STATE STUDENT 1,700 MILES FROM CRIME SCENE, 2ND SUSPECT IN CUSTODY

"USMS Philly is offering an immediate cash reward for Khadfi Fleming, 19, wanted for robbery," the agency wrote on X, adding that Fleming is also a "person of interest" in the Monday attack on the off-duty officer.

Fleming has not been charged in connection with the Monday incident.

But authorities were already looking for the 19-year-old before the latest violence.

Fleming is wanted on a robbery charge connected to the June killing of Billy Schmidt, a 22-year-old Penn State student who was shot while walking home from an NBA Finals watch party.

MANHUNT UNDERWAY AFTER COLLEGE STUDENT FATALLY SHOT CHASING ROBBERS WHO ALLEGEDLY STOLE HIS PHONE

Schmidt was just blocks from his South Philadelphia home when he was fatally shot around 1:30 a.m. on June 6.

Surveillance video captured the final moments before the shooting, with Schmidt heard asking for his stolen phone back before a gunshot rang out.

His father, Bill Schmidt, previously described his son as someone who "cared about everybody and never hurt or bothered a soul."

MANHUNT UNDERWAY FOR KANSAS CITY SHOOTING SPREE SUSPECT NEAR WORLD CUP VENUE; FBI OFFERING $25K REWARD

"For him to get shot like that is a travesty," he told ABC7.

The killing sparked a search for two 16-year-old murder suspects, including Fleming's younger brother.

U.S. Marshals captured Azzubair Outen-Fleming in Colorado Springs, Colorado, about a month after Schmidt's death. Authorities said the teenager was found at a distant relative's home and initially tried to conceal his identity.

Philadelphia Police Department Deputy Commissioner Frank Vanore said Outen-Fleming would face a murder charge, Fox 29 reported.

NEW YORK STATE POLICE LAUNCH MANHUNT AFTER KILLING, HOUSE FIRE FOR 'ARMED AND DANGEROUS' SUSPECT

The second teen, Kaiseem Smith, surrendered to Philadelphia police.

Schmidt was studying digital journalism and media at Penn State and was expected to graduate in December.

Now, two months after his killing, authorities are seeking the elder Fleming as they investigate whether he was involved in the latest violent encounter.

Anyone with information about Fleming's whereabouts is urged to contact the U.S. Marshals Service at 1-866-865-TIPS (8477).

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Philadelphia Police Department and U.S. Marshals Service for additional information and comment.

Fox News Digital's Louis Casiano and Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

item.title: Golfer Hailey Ostrom is Team Sophie, Hilary Duff compares herself to LeBron & pig squealing contests!
item.description: Hilary Duff's viral LeBron James moment on her Lucky Me Tour, Sophie Cunningham's new golf ally, and France's pig-squealing contest are here.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

Over the weekend, I had a conversation with a bartender whose boyfriend just got deployed.

"All I do is work and gym and sit around the apartment feeling sorry for myself because he's not here. I need a hobby," she said. "What do you do for fun?"

I told her maybe I'm not the right person to ask. Because all I do it work and gym as well. Throw in a Saturday trek through the woods here and there.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK

And the hobbies I do have maybe aren't very exciting for a bartender in her early 20s. I'm in a book club, and I've recently become fixated on houseplants. I fear I'm just a couple of knitting needles away from the geriatric trifecta. And in my 30s, no less!

But then what do I run across this morning? A video of Wiz Khalifa absolutely giddy over his houseplants:

I mean, I knew he was pretty fond of at least one particular type of plant (the kind you're not allowed to grow in your house), but I was not expecting Bird of Paradise and Monstera.

So maybe I'm not so uncool after all. Or all of us Millennials are just following the exact same pipeline.

Speaking of, today we're checking in on Millennial Queen Hilary Duff, who is comparing herself to an NBA star. Plus, we've found another Sophie Cunningham ally (certainly not in the WNBA, though), and there's some weird stuff going on in France.

Like, really weird.

Pour yourself a cocktail, drop your work phone into a houseplant, and let's get rolling.

Hilary Duff feels just like LeBron James

I recruited that bartender to my book club, by the way. So there's a win.

Anyway, Hilary Duff went viral during a show on her Lucky Me Tour in Philadelphia Sunday night.

"We started in Florida, went to LA, we've ended up here," she said. "I'm starting to feel like LeBron!"

She had that one in the holster with the safety off. Could not wait to deploy it.

It was cute, though, I laughed. And besides, I'll tolerate no Hilary Duff slander in this column.

I will, however, tolerate LeBron James slander. Actually, as a Pacers fan who had to suffer through his "Big 3" Miami Heat era, I encourage LeBron slander.

Get a load of his agent, Rich Paul, blabbering on about how athletes have "the hardest job in the world."

The hardest job in the world.

Now, look, I get it. Athletes have a physically demanding job, and there's a lot of pressure on them.

There's also a lot of pressure on police officers, brain surgeons, air traffic controllers, school bus drivers... need me to go on?

But this dude (whose name is literally "Rich") thinks that the hardest job in the world is… getting paid millions of dollars to play sports. Just because their family and friends ask them for money. And because $100 million is "really $50 million after taxes."

Let me find my tiny violin.

It reminds me of a time when I worked for the Titans as a social media manager, and the team was going through a particularly tough camp workout. A high-profile player — whom I won't name — said to me on the sideline, "Can we trade jobs? You go do this and I just play with my phone?"

I said, "We trading salaries, too?"

Wide-eyed, he said, "NOPE!" then ran right back onto the field.

That's what I thought.

Hailey Ostrom shows her support for Sophie Cunningham

Sadly, I don't think I'd make it in the NFL. I wouldn't make it in the WNBA, either. The Lord has given me many blessings in life, but height isn't one of them. And I'm pretty sure the last time I played basketball was sometime around the fourth grade, so I'm probably a little rusty.

Look, I am so sick of talking about the WNBA. And I'd say you guys are probably sick of reading about it — but clearly you're not. I see those analytics. WNBA soap opera stories are CLICKERS.

Particularly the ones involving Sophie Cunningham.

And while (seemingly) the entire league is ganging up on Sophie, a new ally has emerged. Golfer Hailey Ostrom has entered the chat.

I am no expert on the hierarchy of golf influencers. You'd have to talk to my colleague Joe Kinsey about that. I am, however, comfortable saying Hailey is in the top 3. I think Paulina Gretzky is in there, too. But I don't think either have dethroned Paige Spiranac.

PAULINA GRETZKY HIT THE GOLF COURSE DRESSED FOR SUCCESS AND WON, BROOKS NADER IN HER BAYWATCH RED & A SQUIRREL

Maybe one day.

Maybe when the WNBA assembles its task force to determine what a woman is, the commish can call in Hailey to testify. Or literally any human being with a brain — which seems to be extra hard to find in that league lately.

Who's signing up for France's annual pig-squealing championship?

Yes, friends, that is a thing. For 43 years running!

Which means that while France was wrestling with inflation, unemployment and political upheaval in the early 1980s, one visionary looked at the state of the nation and thought, "Enough of this. We need to know who does the best pig impression."

A dignified, time-honored and storied tradition was born.

Just look at those patriots making their country proud.

The 2026 installment of this contest took place over the weekend, and a fella named Noel Jamet won — claiming his 10th title. A record!

Some say he's the GOAT of pig squealing. An athlete on par with Michael Jordan, Tom Brady and Serena Williams.

But we'll never know until he takes on the true champion. And my fellow "South Park" fans know exactly who that is.

Let's open the mailbag.

📩 Email: amber.harding@outkick.com (Send your thoughts, stories, tips, rants and photos of your dog.)

🐦 Twitter/X: @TheAmberHarding

📸 Instagram: @amberharding

Caitlyn W. writes: I remember reading in Nightcaps that you were planning to do the HYROX race in Nashville, and I'm convinced you have to know someone to get into one of these things.

Last time I tried, I made an account ahead of time, set a reminder for when registration opened, and was on the website right when tickets went on sale. I even had my husband trying on his laptop at the same time. We both sat in the queue forever, and by the time either of us got through, sold out. I mean WTF.

Amber:

Sounds like me buying Garth Brooks tickets a few weeks ago.

But yeah, I've kind of given up on HYROX for that exact reason. There are plenty of ways to torture myself that don't involve a waitlist.

I actually signed up for a Spartan Super race in October. I've never done one before, so pray for me. I'm not worried about the running part... or the mud or even leaping over fire. It's all the obstacles that I can't practice in my regular gym that I'm worried about.

That and the superhuman grip strength I'm told you have to possess to finish one of these things.

There's a Ninja Warrior gym here in Middle Tennessee. I'm probably going to go there to train at least a few times. Which sounds ridiculous, but I'm committed to not humiliating myself on race day.

But hey, at least I don't have to wear 125 T-shirts.

Remember when I told y'all there's a Guinness World Record for literally everything? There truly is.

Anyway, if anyone has any Spartan training tips, send them my way.

Amber:

Thanks to Drew in Katy, Texas, for passing along.

I can confirm Rocky gives similar mission reports. And thanks to his tireless service, we remain safe from highly camouflaged ground terrorists and insurgent chipmunks.

This is a great Instagram account, by the way.

Gene in the Rock writes: Good boys know what FAFO means...

Fred H. writes: Tate is a cow dog I have who takes his job seriously. I never ask him to come with me to check cows because he's always ready. He feels his job is to look after me. When I give the cows mineral if he thinks they're too close to me he pushes them back. Also Tate, 'I'm not too busy so how about a tummy rub.'

item.title: Inside the New York Jets' revamped performance facility and player development strategy
item.description: The Jets' new Player Performance Center features AI-powered apps, force plates and velocity-based training to personalize player preparation.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: The most important feature of the New York Jets’ next-generation Player Performance Center may be that no single feature defines it.

Jets owner Woody Johnson has invested in growing the facilities by more than double for this upcoming season, as the team looks to turn the page on the 2025 season and make strides in 2026.

"We are investing in an exceptionally dynamic, innovative training staff with experience designing and utilizing advanced performance systems to support our players. Our new facilities will be 250% larger, allowing us to increase training capacity and centralize strength and conditioning, recovery, and nutrition," Johnson said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"We have already implemented state-of-the-art equipment in our temporary facility, granting our team access to some of the most advanced training resources in the league."

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

There will be new technology: vibroacoustic recovery pods, multimodal wellness chambers, pneumatic resistance equipment, computer-vision tracking and a custom-built, AI-powered player performance app.

But when Jets director of player performance Erik Korem describes the project, he repeatedly returns to a broader idea.

"We’re building a holistic health and human performance ecosystem," Korem said. "We’re taking some big steps in our strength and conditioning, nutrition, sports science and recovery departments. The use of data and AI will be part of this, but I think it extends beyond that."

That distinction is the center of the Jets’ Phase 2 renovation at the Atlantic Health Jets Training Center. The team is not just replacing an aging weight room with a larger one. It is redesigning the way players move through the daily cycle of assessment, training, practice, fueling and recovery, all while giving the practitioners responsible for those areas a shared environment in which to work.

The planned two-story performance center will expand the former space by 250%, according to the Jets’ official construction announcement. Its four stated priorities are player performance, recovery, efficient daily flow and the integration of new technology. Dedicated zones will support strength, power, speed and mobility work, while expanded nutrition and recovery areas are intended to make individualized programs easier to deliver.

The investment is already affecting the current roster. During construction, players are working in a temporary training structure with a footprint more than 70% larger than the former weight room. The Jets moved equipment into the interim facility after mandatory minicamp, and demolition of the old space was completed in July. New equipment and technology have been installed in the temporary building rather than held back for the finished center.

That approach reflects an instruction Korem said has come consistently from chairman Woody Johnson, general manager Darren Mougey and head coach Aaron Glenn: The long-term project cannot compromise the team’s short-term preparation.

Korem credited Johnson for his investment in the facility, as they look to translate that investment into on-field results for the 2026 season.

"It just is a reflection of Mr. Johnson's investment," Korem said. "It's only going to help them as individuals and as a team."

The promise of the new center is personalization.

Football teams have never trained every player identically; a 300-pound lineman and a 180-pound defensive back have different jobs, bodies and physical demands. Korem’s goal is to make those distinctions more precise. More frequent assessments, he said, can help the staff identify whether a player needs additional mobility, strength, power, speed work or a change in training volume. The team’s custom app is designed to help organize those inputs and deliver more individualized recommendations.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"The more tools you have and the more appropriate data you have from a serial perspective, you can then develop more specific training programs and interventions for each individual athlete," Korem said. "To me, that’s really where data collection and AI is going to help the field of human performance in general."

The key word is "serial." A force-plate test or motion-capture assessment offers a snapshot; repeated measurements can reveal how an athlete is changing across a week, a training block or a rehabilitation program. Korem said the Jets will expand their use of 3D motion capture, force plates and other telemetry tools to better understand movement and physical readiness.

That approach reflects a wider development in elite sport. A 2025 scoping review indexed by the National Library of Medicine described force plates as one of the most commonly used technologies for monitoring acute changes in athletes’ neuromuscular function. The practical value, however, depends on reliable testing and sound interpretation. Data is useful only when it changes a decision.

The same principle applies inside the rack. Computer vision can track a bar’s path and speed, while connected resistance systems can record ranges and angles and adjust loading as fatigue develops. This is part of a training method often called velocity-based training: Instead of prescribing work only from a previously measured one-repetition maximum, coaches can use the speed of the current lift to judge the quality of the rep and the athlete’s readiness that day. A systematic review of elite-athlete research found that velocity-based resistance training can support strength and power development, while also noting that protocols and results vary.

For the Jets, the technology is meant to sharpen the judgment of coaches, not replace it. The facility can capture more information, and AI can help sort and present it, but the performance staff still has to decide what matters for a particular player on a particular day.

The project also fits a broader organizational move toward analytics. Mougey said in July that the Jets are using AI to automate time-consuming work and help staff digest large amounts of information in scouting and personnel. In that context, the performance app is another expression of the same idea: use automation to make information easier to act on, then leave consequential decisions with football and performance professionals.

Korem describes training and recovery as an arc. Players must first rise into the highly activated state required for lifting, practice and games. Then they must come down from it.

"The recover part is how quickly can they go from being in this highly active state, or what we call a sympathetic state, to getting in this rest-and-digest state," he said.

One of the center’s most distinctive tools, the TERSA SAVA Sound Pod, is designed for that transition. The memory-foam pod surrounds the user with music and low-frequency vibration. TERSA describes the system as combining spatial audio with vibroacoustic frequencies to encourage deep calm. Korem said players have been able to enter a relaxed state quickly in the pod, making it a useful option after demanding work.

The Ammortal Chamber takes a different approach, stacking several modalities into one session. The manufacturer lists red and near-infrared light, pulsed electromagnetic fields and vibroacoustic sound among the chamber’s components. Korem’s interest is partly logistical: If a player can use multiple recovery modalities at once, the intervention may fit more easily into a tightly scheduled NFL day.

These systems are the most futuristic pieces of the renovation, but Korem presents them as additions to a much larger recovery program—not substitutes for foundational work. Training load, sleep, hydration, nutrition and the ability to downshift after practice still form the base. The devices expand the menu available to players and staff.

The same individualized philosophy carries into the kitchen.

Under director of performance nutrition Carmen Spencer, the Jets’ nutrition staff works with team chefs to provide protein, carbohydrates, healthy fats, fruits and vegetables in forms players will actually want to eat. Korem described menus that might include salmon, several chicken preparations and action stations serving items such as poke bowls.

The objective changes with the player and the moment: A whole-grain option may make sense in one meal, while a fast-digesting carbohydrate may be more useful immediately before practice.

"What undergirds all this is: What fuels performance?" Korem said. "What are the things that we need to deliver to the players to help their bodies recover, to help fuel in-game performance and practice performance, and hydration?"

It is an area in which the organization has something to prove. In the NFL Players Association’s 2025 team report card—based on responses from players on 2024 rosters—the Jets ranked 29th overall. Players gave the club a C-minus for food and dining, a D-plus for the locker room and a C-plus for the weight room. They were more positive about the nutritionist/dietitian category, which received a B-plus, and 87 percent said they received an individualized nutrition plan.

The Jets have not publicly characterized the renovation as a response to that survey. Still, the sequence is significant. Phase 1, unveiled in 2025, replaced the locker room with 92 custom lockers and added a redesigned wet area, a larger sauna and a barbershop.

Phase 2 directly addresses the scale and function of the old weight room while expanding nutrition, recovery and performance services. Whatever the motivation, the work creates a visible standard against which players can judge the club’s promise of improvement.

For all the technology going into the building, Korem is direct about the most difficult and important workout of training camp: practice.

The purpose of camp is to prepare players for game demands. Depending on position and role, that can mean building toward 65 to 75 snaps while reaching the necessary speed and volume benchmarks. The weight room supports strength, power, speed, endurance and mobility, but it cannot become the main event once football work intensifies.

"Think about the weight room on the field," Korem said of practice. "There’s qualities that you’re developing on the field. What’s happening in the weight room is you’re supporting" those qualities.

That is also the most realistic way to understand what the Player Performance Center can—and cannot—do. No recovery pod, data platform or force plate can guarantee wins or prevent every injury. What an integrated center can do is give coaches and practitioners more chances to identify needs, individualize work, recover efficiently and keep players available to develop their football skills.

Korem ultimately measures the investment less by the sophistication of the equipment than by the quality of the system around it. Johnson, he said, has supported not only new tools but the hiring of practitioners who know how to use them.

"You can have tools, but do you have the people behind those tools?" Korem said. "It’s the whole ecosystem of the people and the resources that make any type of building come to life."

That may be the defining ambition of the renovation. The Jets are building a much larger performance center, but the competitive bet is on something harder to photograph: better information, shared more quickly, turned into better daily decisions for every player.

item.title: 'Blue Bloods' star Jennifer Esposito says she was locked in psych ward as health battle spiraled
item.description: Jennifer Esposito reveals how celiac disease caused liver failure, a psychiatric ward stay and thoughts of suicide before doctors finally diagnosed her.
item.content:encoded:
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Jennifer Esposito is opening up about the yearslong health battle that she says derailed her career, left her severely depressed and eventually landed her in a psychiatric ward before doctors diagnosed her with celiac disease.

During an appearance on Maria Menounos' "Heal Squad" podcast, Esposito, 53, recalled being a young actress in New York City when unexplained physical and mental health problems became so debilitating that she was forced to put her life on hold.

"I had a whole life beginning in the city, and I was a young actor and I had to stop everything," Esposito said.

MAYIM BIALIK DETAILS 'NIGHTMARE' AFTER ONE INJECTION OF GLP-1 DRUG LED TO WEEKS OF DEBILITATING SIDE EFFECTS

The actress said she became "deeply depressed" and began having "thoughts of suicide" as doctors struggled to determine what was wrong.

"They brought me to a psychologist, like they had me on every medication," she recalled. "They wanted to give me shock treatment at one point because I wasn't responding. I'm very sensitive to medication. It was a really bad time. And my mother had people pray over me."

Esposito said she eventually began to suspect that her physical and mental health symptoms could be connected to nutrition.

"I realized that there was a major connection with what I was eating and my vitamins and then my body," she said.

DAMON WAYANS REVEALS THE SCARY SYMPTOM THAT LED TO HIS TYPE 2 DIABETES DIAGNOSIS

Her health began to "collapse" while she was working on the ABC comedy "Samantha Who?," which aired from 2007 to 2009, according to the actress.

Esposito recalled experiencing alarming physical symptoms, including losing her hair and fingernails.

"I had hair falling out, nails falling off," she said.

Then, she said, a tooth fell out while she was filming a scene.

CARLY SIMON REVEALS THE COMMON CONDITION THAT MASKED HER PARKINSON'S DIAGNOSIS

"A tooth fell out of my mouth, like literally in the middle of a scene," Esposito recalled. "I was mortified but also had been so ill that I just — I went hysterical. Like, somebody has to help me."

Esposito said she was misdiagnosed several times, with doctors considering conditions including multiple sclerosis and irritable bowel syndrome. She said a therapist suggested stress was behind her symptoms.

"Talk about gaslighting," she said.

"We don't ever treat the actual underlying issue. We treat symptoms in this country, in America," Esposito continued. "I went for years on that, and I tried everything myself. I went to holistic healers. I went to get my aura cleansed. I was vegan."

Desperate for answers, Esposito said she began attending a non-denominational church in an effort to "feel recharged."

On one drive there, she recalled reaching a breaking point.

"I remember saying to myself, because I was so depressed of being so sick all the time and fighting panic disorders … ‘If you don't get a diagnosis, you have to accept the fact that you're crazy, and you've created this, and you're going to let it go because I can't keep doing this.’"

Moments later, she said, a large piece of wood flew from a truck in front of her and smashed through her windshield.

RANDY TRAVIS' HEALTH CRISIS BEGAN WITH 'CONGESTION' AND ENDED IN A FIVE-MONTH HOSPITAL STAY

"I'm sitting with glass all over me," Esposito said. After managing to pull to the side of the road, she took the frightening accident as a sign to continue looking for answers.

Two days later, Esposito said, a doctor called with her diagnosis: celiac disease.

"I’m not sure how you’re alive," Esposito recalled the doctor telling her.

According to Esposito, her case was so severe that her liver was failing.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition in which consuming gluten — a protein found in wheat, barley and rye — triggers an immune response that damages the small intestine. That damage can interfere with the body's ability to absorb nutrients and can cause symptoms extending well beyond the digestive system, including fatigue, anemia, neurological problems and elevated liver enzymes. A strict, lifelong gluten-free diet is the primary treatment and can allow the intestine to heal, according to the Mayo Clinic.

After receiving her diagnosis, Esposito immediately eliminated gluten from her diet, but said her body was in such poor condition that her recovery was grueling.

She recalled being severely deficient in vitamin D and developing welts when exposed to sunlight. Her nervous system was also so overwhelmed, she said, that ordinary stimulation became difficult to tolerate.

"They had me on four Klonopin a day, and I was still a trembling mess," Esposito said. "I was literally sleeping in my kitchen because it was the only place that didn't have a window, because the light — the stimulus from the light — would make me tremble and shake."

'GAME OF THRONES' ACTRESS SAYS SHE JOINED A WELLNESS CULT THAT LED TO A PSYCHOTIC BREAK

"It was horrendous," she added.

About two months after her diagnosis, Esposito began seeing a medical expert who she said wanted to study her because of the severity of her case.

She underwent regular blood and urine testing, but during one appointment, Esposito said she was in such distress that she pleaded with the doctor to keep her in the hospital.

"Doctor, you got to keep me here because I'm jumping out of my skin. I'm going to jump out the window," she recalled saying.

Esposito said the remark was interpreted as a threat of self-harm.

Within half an hour, she said, she was taken to a psychiatric ward under the alias "Betty Franklin."

"I will say it was seven of the most excruciating hours of my entire life because I was yet again pleading for my sanity," she said.

Esposito said her father was with her and recalled fearing that she would not get out if he left.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"If you leave me here, I'm dying because I'm going to fight these people," she recalled thinking.

The actress said the experience became even more frightening when a doctor asked her father for permission to restrain her if she got "out of hand."

Esposito forced herself to remain calm. "I thought, if I ever get out of here, I have to do something," she said.

After returning home, Esposito said she took an increasingly active role in understanding her condition and recovery.

"If you heal your gut, I promise you, not everything can go away," she said, adding that recovery "takes time."

Esposito, who said she now lives outside the United States, told Menounos that she no longer experiences panic attacks and has adopted a dramatically different pace of life.

"This is my life. I get to enjoy time," she said. "I sit down and eat lunch. I sit down and talk to people. There's no phones on the tables."

"There’s a grace given for enjoyment in life," Esposito continued. "I just think we've lost the plot with that. And no wonder why we're all sick."

Looking back on the ordeal, Esposito said she ultimately views her diagnosis as something that changed the trajectory of her life.

"Celiac disease saved my life. One hundred percent," she said.

Esposito said she believes the years of stress and living in "fight or flight" would eventually have taken an even greater toll had her illness not forced her to change course.

"I 100% would have been somewhere not good," she said.

Now, she said, she is "very, very, very clear and grateful" — including for the opportunity her experience has given her to help others.

item.title: Babylon Bee sues New Mexico officials over law requiring AI disclaimers on political satire
item.description: The Babylon Bee sued over New Mexico's AI disclaimer law, arguing HB 182 forces warning labels on political satire and violates free speech.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX — Should political satire come with a warning label?

A New Mexico law requiring disclaimers on certain AI-generated political content, including parody and satire, is being challenged in court by Christian satire news site The Babylon Bee. 

HB 182, passed in 2024, amended New Mexico’s Campaign Reporting Act to add disclosure requirements for political advertisements containing what the law defines as "materially deceptive media." The law mandates that relevant images, video or audio manipulated or created through artificial intelligence must display a prominent AI disclaimer identifying the content as created or manipulated by artificial intelligence.

The Bee, which frequently pokes fun at political candidates and issues, argues the state law violates fundamental free speech rights and due process. 

On Tuesday, the humor site filed a lawsuit against state officials, with the help of the legal organization Alliance Defending Freedom ("ADF"), arguing that the law chills their speech and destroys the intent of comedy.

TENNESSEE MAN JAILED 37 DAYS OVER FACEBOOK MEME MOCKING CHARLIE KIRK'S DEATH WINS $850K SETTLEMENT

"This disclaimer alters the content of the satire and parody The Bee wants to express by alerting the viewer to the satirical or parodical nature of the communication and thereby depriving the expression of its rhetorical force," the complaint states. "Put simply, HB 182 spoils the joke as it begins, each and every time." The website says it is not willing to publish content with the mandated label because it would alter its message.

Seth Dillon, CEO of The Babylon Bee, told Fox News Digital that the law's disclosure requirement imposes a "deeper problem" of compelled speech.

"New Mexico is stuffing words into our mouths, forcing us to say things we wouldn’t say otherwise," he explained.

Just this past week, the Bee posted a satirical AI-generated travel advertisement mocking the Democratic "utopia" of New Mexico and the state's Supreme Court justice David K. Thomson, who will appear on the November ballot. In the fake advertisement, an AI-generated video of Thomson announces the court rules "against the Second Amendment, the First Amendment or any other amendment that lets people do things."

THOMAS, GORSUCH TARGET LANDMARK RULING TRUMP SAYS PROTECTS THE 'FAKE NEWS'

The Bee argued it intends to create content with AI that parodies or satirizes other candidates or ballot questions in the state's elections. Dillon said, though they have not faced penalties yet, they are suing preemptively to protect their rights.

"The concern is real, but we don't censor ourselves," Dillon told Fox News Digital. "If a joke we want to tell is likely to violate the law, we'll tell it, anyway — both because we have a right to, and we refuse to do the tyrant's work for him. If penalties are imposed, we'll sue to defend our rights. In this case, we're suing preemptively to settle the matter before it escalates to that point."

AI CHATBOTS TAKE HEAT OVER LEFT-WING BIAS: ‘NO LONGER BE CONSIDERED NEUTRAL’

The Bee and ADF also argue the law discriminates based on content, by giving a blanket exemption for content appearing in news stories or editorials while entertainment, satire, parody, cartoons and memes are restricted.

The complaint names the seven members of the New Mexico Ethics Commission, which enforces the challenged provisions, as defendants, and calls on the court to issue injunctions preventing enforcement. The filing also claims that individual violations of the law can draw fines up to $1,000 and those can total up to $20,000 with additional violations.

"The government cannot decide which political speech is allowed and which is forbidden," ADF Chief Legal Counsel Jim Campbell told Fox News Digital. "Whenever government officials determine what political speech is acceptable, dissent disappears and democracy suffers. So what we're arguing here is that the First Amendment ensures that the Babylon Bee and anyone else in New Mexico can continue to post political ads and political messages — including satire and parody, addressing some of the most important political questions facing the people of New Mexico."

Campbell noted that concerns about the legislation also came from Democratic state officials.

Upon signing HB 182, Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham wrote that portions of the bill were ambiguous and could "pose legal issues."

The complaint also cites an advisory opinion issued by Attorney General Raúl Torrez in July 2025, concluding that HB 182's disclaimer requirement on satire and parody was "likely unconstitutional on its face."

Fox News Digital reached out to Grisham's office for comment but did not immediately hear back.

The New Mexico Ethics Commission called the lawsuit "baseless" in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Babylon Bee’s pre-enforcement lawsuit is baseless," a spokesperson said. "The Commission has never taken action to enforce the AI-disclaimer requirements in Section 1-19-26.4 of the Campaign Reporting Act, much less for political parody and satire. While the Babylon Bee has a First Amendment right to mock New Mexico, it does not have a right to extract attorneys’ fees from the State."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Alliance Defending Freedom has represented the Babylon Bee in other lawsuits challenging similar censorship laws in Hawaii and California against deepfakes and political satire. The laws were struck down after courts ruled in each case that the state laws were unconstitutional.

Campbell said they will continue to fight similar legislation as it crops up around the country.

"We're trying to ensure that political debate remains robust and that the government doesn't tell its citizens which political speech is allowed," Campbell said.

"We need for people to be allowed to express their views and, ultimately, we need political debate and discourse to be open and free so that the American people can determine what's best for our country moving forward," he added.

item.title: Parents speak out after son with autism, 6, was suspended for biting sandwich into shape of gun
item.description: Kristin and Juan "Ricky" Medina told Fox News Digital their son’s autism can make social norms difficult to understand as they push for less severe discipline.
item.content:encoded:
The parents of a Georgia first-grader with autism are speaking out after their son was suspended for biting his sandwich into the shape of a gun and pointing it at a classmate during lunch, arguing that the school's strict disciplinary policies fail to account for his developmental disabilities.

John Medina, 6, was suspended last March while in first grade at Sarah Harp Elementary School in Fayette County, south of Atlanta. He was diagnosed with level 1 autism at age 4 and later diagnosed with ADHD, conditions his parents say can make it difficult for him to understand social norms.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, parents Kristin and Juan "Ricky" Medina said that John is exceptionally advanced academically, but the school's apparent strict policies and initial lack of developmental assistance have led to roughly 15 suspensions and more than two dozen disciplinary actions since 2023. They added that while some incidents justified escalation, other harmless acts, such as hunting drawings and hand-gun gestures, have also drawn school discipline and scrutiny.

The disciplinary history has ultimately taken a toll on John's self-esteem, especially as he already struggles to make friends and often feels isolated, his parents said. They said their son refers to himself as a "bad kid" because of how he feels he is treated by his peers and the school environment.

10-YEAR-OLD BOY RECOUNTS NEAR-DROWNING AS FAMILY REVEALS FRIENDSHIP WITH CALIFORNIA TEEN LIFEGUARD HERO

Kristin said she was initially shocked to learn that John had been suspended over the sandwich incident, questioning the school's reported "strike" system, in which minor actions such as making a hand gesture or saying the word "gun" can escalate to suspension.

"It was upsetting for me to hear that it was, that is what he was getting in trouble for," Kristin said.

"I felt like they were cracking down more on small stuff, you know, stuff that maybe he didn't need to be suspended for," Ricky added.

While John has been involved in physical incidents, including pushing another student in PE and hitting a classmate with a branch, his parents said many official disciplinary actions stemmed from what they considered harmless hand gestures. Other standard behaviors, like drawing a pilgrim shooting a turkey for Thanksgiving, also drew intense school scrutiny, they said.

They added that weapon-related topics are specifically not discussed in their home, but said they cannot control the outside influences John encounters. They added that children can naturally develop an imaginative fascination with weapons, but John’s autism makes it more difficult for him to filter his speech in the way other children might.

MONTANA TEEN THROWS LASSO TO MAN IN YELLOWSTONE RIVER IN SPLIT-SECOND RESCUE

They also stressed that, because of his autism, traditional punishments are ineffective and could inadvertently reinforce the idea that saying the word "gun" will allow him to leave school when he is having a bad day.

"Instead of singling him out, just make it a teachable moment for him. Teach, ‘Hey, we don't do this in school because of this reason, it's not appropriate,’" Kristin said.

However, the family said they initially faced pushback from the school over developmental accommodations. Kristin said the school initially refused to grant John an Individualized Education Program (IEP), because he was too academically advanced and officials "didn't see" his autism.

According to Kristin, it took about a year and a half, 10 to 12 suspensions and a second evaluation that resulted in an ADHD diagnosis before the school approved his IEP.

John’s parents said they worry that repeatedly focusing on what they consider harmless childhood behavior has reinforced a negative self-image and made him increasingly eager to leave school. John is hesitant to attend school because he believes people are "going to laugh at him for making wrong choices," his parents said.

"I just want to see John start to get his self-esteem built up, his confidence built up, friendships built up," Kristin said. "I don't want him to continue to feel singled out."

The parents said John thankfully finished the previous school year strong, reading at a third-grade level and coming just four test points short of qualifying for the gifted and talented program.

The school also appeared to ease up on suspensions recently, particularly after the family hired Donna Reynolds, a special education advocate, to represent them during school meetings.

John is also currently on a behavioral plan that includes an aide during unstructured periods, including lunch, recess and PE. He also spends time in a smaller, calmer classroom setting, where his parents said he performs exceptionally well.

"What I want to see is that there's less severe punishment like suspensions," Ricky said. "And just continue to talk through things so you can have opportunities to learn from things and maybe focus on real serious concerns."

Fox News Digital reached out to Fayette County Public Schools, the school district under which John's school falls, about his situation. The district declined to go into specific details, but encouraged a review of John's "complete disciplinary history and the full context surrounding the situation rather than focusing on one isolated event."

item.title: Parents of Idaho massacre victim face daily nightmare while demanding death penalty after shock plea twist
item.description: Kristi and Steve Goncalves reveal their daily grief as Bryan Kohberger attempts to withdraw his guilty plea in the University of Idaho murders.
item.content:encoded:
The parents of University of Idaho student Kaylee Goncalves opened up about the daily reality of losing their daughter, revealing their morning thoughts and nightly prayers since her murder.

Speaking on the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast, Kristi and Steve Goncalves detailed their emotional struggle as convicted killer Bryan Kohberger attempts to withdraw his guilty plea in the murders of four University of Idaho students in 2022.

"The first thing every single morning I often ask myself: Is this going to be forever? Will this eventually end? Will it eventually, will it not be the first thing that I think about when I open my eyes?" Kristi told host Sean Hannity.

KAYLEE GONCALVES' MOTHER SAYS FAMILY READY FOR TRIAL AFTER BRYAN KOHBERGER SEEKS TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA

"But at this point I've learned that it's just the new way of life," she added.

Kaylee Goncalves was one of four University of Idaho students killed in November 2022. Bryan Kohberger pleaded guilty in July 2025 to four counts of first-degree murder and one count of felony burglary as part of a deal that spared him the death penalty. He has since sought to withdraw his guilty plea.

Goncalves' father, Steve, added that every night, Kristi hopes their daughter visits her in her dreams so she can tell Kaylee she loves her.

"First and foremost, before she goes to bed, she's praying that Kaylee comes and visits her. She wants to have a conversation. She wants to talk to her. She wants to tell her she loves her. She wants to say everything that we can't say," Steve said.

IDAHO MURDERS: NEW BOOK ON KOHBERGER REVEALS PREVIOUSLY UNSEEN EVIDENCE, CLAIMS SHEATH COULD BE INADMISSIBLE

"Then if you don't have that dream, you wake up disappointed that you didn't have a dream about your baby and had that conversation, and then you just try to fake through it," he added.

Kohberger is now seeking to withdraw the guilty plea that spared him the death penalty for the murders of Goncalves, Madison Mogen, Ethan Chapin and Xana Kernodle. He was sentenced to four consecutive life sentences in prison without the possibility of parole, plus 10 years for burglary.

IDAHO MURDERS EVIDENCE LEAK TRIGGERS CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION FOR INSIDER WHO SPILLED SECRETS: REPORT

In his post-conviction challenge, Kohberger argues he received ineffective assistance of counsel and was manipulated by his court-appointed attorneys into accepting the deal. He also alleges he was led to believe the deal would give him better prison conditions, and he now maintains that he is innocent.

The Goncalves family said Kohberger's attempt to withdraw his plea has been difficult for them after years of legal proceedings, but Kristi Goncalves said his latest challenge could provide another opportunity for prosecutors to pursue the death penalty.

"God is looking out for us," Kristi said. "And maybe this is because the first time around, it was wrong. And this time around, he's going to make sure it's done right, you know — and that is the death penalty."

item.title: Wisconsin Democratic chair dodges on Francesca Hong's Thanksgiving remarks, Tiffany campaign sounds alarm
item.description: Wisconsin Democratic Party chair Devin Remiker dodged questions about Francesca Hong's cancel Thanksgiving controversy, pivoting to attack Republican Tom Tiffany instead.
item.content:encoded:
Wisconsin Democratic Party chair Devin Remiker repeatedly dodged questions about Thanksgiving on Tuesday after state gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, reversed her statement about canceling the holiday.

CNN host John Berman asked Remiker what his personal feelings were about Thanksgiving.

"I love Thanksgiving," Remiker said. "I even host a Friendsgiving every year, so I basically do Thanksgiving twice."

"I think Tom Tiffany is going to have a hard time at Thanksgiving this year after he's lost the governor‘s race, because those sweet potatoes he's looking at remind him of the spray tan of the president that cost him his election," he added.

Berman then asked about how "annoying" it was to have to field questions about Thanksgiving "because Francesca Hong, the candidate who could win the Democratic primary for governor there, has made statements sort of against Thanksgiving and then reversed it. But how much of a problem is this?"

SOCIALIST FRONTRUNNER IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER 'CANCEL THANKSGIVING' POST EMERGES ONLINE

The Wisconsin Democratic Party chair claimed it was giving his party an opportunity to argue that Rep. Tom Tiffany, R-Wis., would make the holiday more expensive.

"I think it's great that we have so many opportunities to talk about how Tom Tiffany is going to make Thanksgiving more expensive for Wisconsinites by driving up the cost of the groceries that it costs to make it, the cost of the gas that it takes to drive to your family's place and gather under one roof to share in a great holiday. So, as many times as I get to hammer that point, I'm more than happy to do it," Remiker responded.

Berman told Remiker he appreciated the "effort" in his reply.

‘COMMON SENSE AGAINST CRAZY’: TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATE SOUNDS ALARM ON SOCIALIST HONG IN WISCONSIN RACE

Hong is among seven Democrats on the ballot in the state's gubernatorial primary Tuesday, including Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley. Tiffany faces Andy Manske in the Republican primary.

"The Democratic Party of Wisconsin capitulated to socialism, and now they’re stuck supporting a socialist who wants to abolish the police, abolish prisons, cancel Thanksgiving, and make Wisconsin the highest-income-taxed state in the nation," a Tiffany campaign spokesperson told Fox News Digital in a statement. 

"While they defend higher taxes, more spending, and fewer jobs, Tom Tiffany will stay focused on making Wisconsin more affordable, keeping our communities safe, and creating more opportunities for everyone."

LEFT’S LATEST SOCIALIST DARLING DRAGGED OVER ‘WHITENESS’ COMMENTS PULLING IN HER OWN FAMILY: ‘WEIRDO RACISM’

Hong said in an interview last week that Thanksgiving was her favorite holiday, reversing a position she held in 2020.

"My favorite holiday is Thanksgiving," Hong told Politico Playbook. "Yep, I don't want to cancel it. I actually love it." Politico wrote in an X post that Hong was joking.

"You know, I'm just ... I'm going to be real," Hong said. "I'm kind of a curmudgeon when it comes to holidays in general."

Hong was responding to the backlash she faced for a deleted post, which was initially made on X in November 2020, after she appeared to draw comparisons between the deadly pandemic and the Thanksgiving holiday.

"Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621," Hong wrote at the time. 

Fox News' Lindsay Kornick contributed to this report.

item.title: Socialist Wisconsin governor candidate referred to America as 'abundance of suffering,' resurfaced post shows
item.description: Fox News Digital found Francesca Hong's X posts calling America "an abundance of suffering" and urging police abolition in her governor campaign.
item.content:encoded:
A socialist candidate for governor in Wisconsin with an extensive history of inflammatory online posts once described America as "an abundance of suffering," Fox News Digital has found.

"I want this country to stop being an abundance of suffering but a wealth of opportunity," reads a Jan. 20, 2022 X post from Wisconsin state Rep. Francesca Hong, who is running in the Democratic Party's primary election to become the state's top official.

"We can do this by providing equal rights to Black and Brown folks," the post continues. "Elect more Black and Brown folks who won't be racist obstructionists. We can all be better and do so much more."

SOCIALIST FRONTRUNNER IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER 'CANCEL THANKSGIVING' POST EMERGES ONLINE

This isn't the first time the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidate has faced scrutiny for past comments on social media that are especially critical of America and its institutions and ideals.

"Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621," Hong wrote in a now-deleted post on X.

"If it takes a worldwide pandemic for us to realize we should stop celebrating colonialism and the original superspreader event that killed indigenous folx [sic] and women, so be it," she added, referring to the spread of smallpox that killed many indigenous Americans.

Despite a string of posts, the former chef and mother-of-one, is now running for the Democratic nomination for governor in Wisconsin. She's the latest in a strong of socialists seeking statewide or federal office in this year's primary against establishment Democrats.

LEFT’S LATEST SOCIALIST DARLING DRAGGED OVER ‘WHITENESS’ COMMENTS PULLING IN HER OWN FAMILY: ‘WEIRDO RACISM’

Hong, who is Korean America, also said in a 2019 post that she was anxious in the company of White people.

"I ate two bites of my kid's cheeseburger at a Culver's in black river falls and told him they ran out of ice cream," that post said. "Mostly just wanted to leave bc I was on the verge of a anxiety attack...to (sic) many old white people who didn't think we spoke english."

When prosecutors declined to press charges in 2021 for the high-profile shooting of Jacob Blake in August 2020, in Kenosha, Wisc., Hong joined the chorus of left-wing voicing calling to abolish police.

"How is 7 bullets in the back not excessive force," she said at the time. "Police exist to uphold White supremacy. Defund then abolish. Reform can't be an option. My heart breaks for the trauma the Blake family and their community continues to endure."

TOP WISCONSIN DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST CANDIDATE CONFRONTED ON PAST 'DEFUND POLICE' RHETORIC

Hong's team declined in July to walk back her position on police.

"Rep. Hong has spoken in the past about police and prison abolition as an aspirational goal, akin to eradicating disease or eliminating poverty," a spokesperson told Fox News Digital at the time. "Her values haven’t changed, but the way she talks about this issue has."

Hong has acknowledged that the governor does not have the power to defund the police.

The candidate brushed off the scrutiny of her posts when asked about them by Fox News Digital ahead of her primary election on Tuesday, saying she wanted to be a sports journalist in college.

"I learned then you have some hot takes, and sometimes bad takes on Twitter, and I let my feelings out into the world," Hong said.

FRANCESCA HONG ASKED ABOUT LACK OF AOC ENDORSEMENT AND THE HOUSE DEM'S REMARK ABOUT THE 'WOKE 1' ERA

She said she was focused on issues voters are concerned about.

Hong's campaign did not return a request for comment on the latest post uncovered by Fox News Digital.

Fox News' CJ Womack and Paul Steinhouser contributed to this report.

item.title: Former Wisconsin Gov Scott Walker warns Hong ‘undermining one of her strengths’ with campaign backtracking
item.description: Former Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker warns about democratic socialist Francesca Hong's rise as both parties scramble to stop her primary momentum.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE — Former Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker shared his concerns about politics in the state amid the rise of democratic socialist Francesca Hong, while also arguing she's "undermining" her own campaign in a Fox News Digital interview on Tuesday.

Hong, a Wisconsin state representative, is leading the field heading into Tuesday's Democratic primary, according to recent polling. The far-left, 37-year-old former chef and single mother has courted controversy in recent weeks for her progressive platform and past rhetoric about abolishing the police, as well as her hot take on Thanksgiving.

"Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621," Hong wrote in a now-deleted November 2020 post to X. "If it takes a worldwide pandemic for us to realize we should stop celebrating colonialism and the original superspreader event that killed indigenous folx [sic] and women, so be it," she added. She has since said her views have "evolved," telling Politico Thanksgiving is actually her "favorite" holiday.

"Well one, I think it’s a sign she’ll say just about anything to get elected," Walker, who is now the president of Young America's Foundation, told Fox News Digital ahead of Tuesday’s primary. "And finally, as she’s getting close, thinking she might actually be the nominee, people are telling her you cannot have outrageously outlandish ideas."

WISCONSIN DEM SOCIALIST GUBERNATORIAL HOPEFUL DODGES WHETHER SHE STILL WANTS TO 'ABOLISH POLICE'

"Not only on Thanksgiving. Doesn’t care for Christmas. Heck, in Wisconsin, doesn’t like Culver’s cheese curds," Walker said, in reference to another of Hong's old social media posts. "Those are all things that are wildly out of touch with the people that she’s going to need if she’s got a shot for the general election."

Walker warned Hong, however, that she could be hurting her campaign because primary voters had been attracted to her, in part, because of her bucking of the Democratic establishment.

"But I think she’s undermining one of her strengths," Walker said. "One of the reasons why she’s going to win today’s primary is because Democratic primary voters view her as not the establishment, not the traditional politician. Someone who will just tell it like it is, even if people don’t agree with her. So the more she backtracks on things she didn’t even say as a kid — she’s actually posted as an elected official — the more I think she starts to undermine her own base, and the typical voter can see right through her." 

Fox News Digital reached out to the Hong campaign for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Walker is the most recent Republican to serve as Wisconsin governor. He was elected in 2010 and 2014 — and also survived a recall in 2012 — before losing to Democrat Tony Evers during a bid for a third term in 2018.

SOCIALIST FRONTRUNNER IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER 'CANCEL THANKSGIVING' POST EMERGES ONLINE

Establishment Democrats have been hoping to stop Hong in her tracks, but she's the clear polling favorite going into Tuesday night. David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive who earned the endorsement of outgoing Gov. Evers, told Politico that Republicans wanted Hong to be their opponent.

"You know, it’s the only time that I know that the governor — Tony Evers — the Republican Governors Association and Turning Point USA have ever been on the same page: in thinking that Francesca Hong is the best candidate to lose this race," Crowley said.

Whoever wins Tuesday's Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial primary will face Trump ally Tom Tiffany, who is heavily favored in the Republican primary.

Hong has pushed back on the narrative that she’s too extreme, although she has conspicuously failed to win the endorsement of even far-left darling Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt.

"We have to take this moment, a movement moment, and be bold with transformative change, and build the actual big tent that we can, and we must be as Democrats," Hong told a crowd at a senior community center in Siren.

"It’s common sense versus dangerously crazy," Walker told Fox News Digital of the recent rise of democratic socialism in the U.S. "When you talk about abolishing the police, when you talk about a world without prisons, no consequences for criminals, no push for public safety."

SCOTT WALKER: DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ARE COMING FOR MY STATE. THIS IS HOW WE BEAT THEM

SCOTT WALKER: DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ARE COMING FOR MY STATE. THIS IS HOW WE BEAT THEM

Walker said it is intriguing timing that next year will be the 40th anniversary of President Ronald Reagan’s "Tear down this wall" speech at the Berlin Wall.

"In all the years since, I think we’ve kind of lost a sense in America, of why there was a wall there in the first place, why did it have to come down," he said. "That’s because communism and democratic socialism are barriers to freedom. They’re barriers to economic freedom, political freedom, even religious freedom. That’s why Ronald Reagan, Pope John Paul II, Margaret Thatcher and others fought so hard to bring that down. We have to remind anyone, but particularly young people, that democratic socialism has failed in Venezuela, just like communism failed in the old Soviet Union. And it’s a really important reminder."

Walker said the newfound popularity of democratic socialism is in part due to primary voters shifting to the left, particularly under President Donald Trump. Second, he said, is the "years of liberal indoctrination on college campuses." The third, he argued, is due to a strong frustration over housing prices and the feeling that young adults' "piece of the American dream is slipping away," so they are drifting toward the extremes on either side of the aisle.

item.title: Costco employee fatally rammed car into co-worker on motorcycle after seeing hug: DA
item.description: Tyler Sorensen allegedly rammed his car into co-worker Jonathon Langdon's motorcycle in an Issaquah Costco parking lot out of jealousy over a hug.
item.content:encoded:
A Costco employee in a Seattle suburb allegedly rammed his car into a co-worker riding a motorcycle, killing him out of anger and jealousy, according to reports citing statements made to investigators.

Tyler Sorensen, 22, is charged with second-degree murder in connection with the July 31 death of 20-year-old Jonathon Langdon in Issaquah.

Sorensen allegedly followed Langdon out of a Costco parking lot before swerving into his lane and striking his motorcycle, according to court documents obtained by Fox News Digital.

SILICON VALLEY DEVELOPER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER INVESTIGATORS SAY TESLA REACHED 142 MPH BEFORE FATAL CRASH

Langdon was thrown from his motorcycle into a metal signpost, authorities said. Sorensen fled the scene but returned an hour later with a family member to speak with investigators, according to the Issaquah Police Department.

Sorensen told his father that he "did something stupid" and had been in a collision but kept going. Once his father realized that Sorensen had left the scene of an accident, he drove his son back to the collision site an hour after the deadly incident, prosecutors said. 

Sorensen allegedly told investigators that he became jealous after seeing Langdon hug a female co-worker whom Sorensen claimed was his girlfriend. After seeing the hug, he texted friends that his "blood is boiling."

SEATTLE POLICE CHIEF SNAPS OVER CHICAGO HOME QUESTIONS, ABSENCE FROM CITY AFTER MASS SHOOTING

Sorensen allegedly told investigators that he and the female co-worker had been in a relationship for about two to three months, which ended in late May. However, she told police that they had never dated and that she only considered him a friend and had repeatedly told him she "needed space" and that he was "crossing boundaries," authorities said. 

Sorensen allegedly told law enforcement that his actions were "stupid" and that he only wanted to "spook" Langdon.

"Our hearts go out to the family and friends of the victim as they process this tragic loss of life," said Issaquah Police Chief Steve Mylett.

item.title: NYPD’s legendary ‘Hip-Hop Cop' Derrick Parker, who investigated rap’s biggest stars and murders, dead at 65
item.description: Derrick Parker, the NYPD's "Hip-Hop Cop" who investigated cases tied to Tupac Shakur, Notorious B.I.G. and Jam Master Jay, has died at age 65.
item.content:encoded:
Derrick Parker, the former NYPD detective known as the "Hip-Hop Cop" for his work in the city's rap-related intelligence unit in the 1990s, has died. He was 65.

His brother, Ralph, told Fox News Digital Monday he died unexpectedly on July 24 at a hospital in New York's Nassau County. He did not give a cause.

A funeral is scheduled for Thursday at the J Foster Phillips Funeral Home in Jamaica, New York.

Derrick J. Parker was the former head of the NYPD's rap intelligence unit when the city's hip-hop scene exploded in popularity in the 1990s. His work included monitoring high-profile artists and their entourages as they came and went from the Big Apple. He said he shared his strategies to reduce violence in the music industry in other parts of the country, including in Miami and Atlanta.

TUPAC SHAKUR MURDER SUSPECT TAKES CENTER STAGE AT TRIAL NEARLY 30 YEARS AFTER SHOOTING SHOCKED MUSIC WORLD

He also served as a homicide and cold case detective during a career that spanned more than 20 years and worked alongside the US Marshals, the ATF, the DEA and the FBI, according to his website.

"You have to watch and see who's coming to your city. Who's there and who's what," he told Fox News Digital in a 2024 interview. "We can't track everybody, but when certain people come to the city, you should know who, especially certain people that are on your radar. That's the way I look at it."

FIRST ON FOX: A Senate Republican leading a dive into Dr. Anthony Fauci’s old government iPhone alleged that "career bureaucrats" within Fauci’s old agency are sabotaging the senator’s and others’ quest for information from the pandemic era.

FAUCI HELD IN CONTEMPT AS COVID CELLPHONE LANDS IN HANDS OF SENATE INVESTIGATORS

On Monday, Johnson’s panel, the Senate Homeland Security Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, released the first tranche of private messages found on the device, which included over 34,000 text messages and 522 voicemails.

The first batch of texts, exchanged between Fauci and former Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Dr. Rochelle Walensky and Dr. Vivek Murthy, who would become surgeon general under the Biden administration, revealed that Fauci had concerns about the effects of the second dose of mRNA vaccines on pregnant women in the first trimester.

FAUCI'S HHS IPHONE TURNED OVER TO SENATE INVESTIGATORS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

"I asked around a bit more and another issue came up that you need to be aware of," Fauci wrote. "Since many people have significant cytokines storm and fever after the 2nd dose, this theoretically could be associated with miscarriage in the 1st trimester."

The lawmaker believed that the revelation was just the "tip of the iceberg," but has remained cautious with his investigation and what information dumps come next, particularly to protect the personal information of others who may be included in the communications.

FAUCI IN THE HOT SEAT AS GOP SENATOR TEARS INTO 'TRULY SICK' VACCINE TEXTS: 'TIP OF THE ICEBERG'

He argued that releasing the first batch of texts was based on public health and safety concerns, said that Fauci’s concern "immediately impacts public safety, immediately impacts informed consent."

item.title: Dangerous drug-resistant fungus spreads across US, reaching 27 states
item.description: Thousands of Candida auris cases have been reported across 27 states in 2026, with the drug-resistant fungus posing deadly risks in healthcare settings.
item.content:encoded:
Thousands of cases of a potentially deadly, drug-resistant fungus have been reported across 27 states so far this year, according to provisional CDC data.

As of the week ending July 25, a total of 3,437 clinical cases of Candida auris (C. auris) had been documented in the U.S. so far in 2026.

California accounts for 873 cases — roughly one-quarter of the country’s total. Other states with high numbers include Texas (433), Tennessee (283), Ohio (279), Georgia (193), Louisiana (179), Illinois (171), Arizona (171), Michigan (146), Virginia (132) and Pennsylvania (121), per the CDC.

EXPERTS REVEAL HOW TO AVOID DEADLY LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE AS NYC OUTBREAK KILLS 5

The remaining states have fewer than 100 cases each.

Candida auris is a type of yeast that can cause serious infections, primarily in hospitals, nursing homes and other healthcare settings.

The fungus, which can survive on surfaces for prolonged periods, is "highly transmissible between patients through contact with contaminated surfaces or objects," the CDC states. It can spread through contaminated items such as bedrails, doorknobs and shared medical equipment.

C. auris can also be spread by people who carry the fungus but do not show symptoms, known as "colonization."

Clinical cases do not necessarily represent infections. The CDC defines a clinical case as detection of C. auris in a specimen collected during the normal course of medical care. 

Some clinical specimens can come from sites where the presence of C. auris may represent colonization rather than a true infection.

The health effects of the fungus can range from colonization without symptoms to potentially deadly invasive infections, including bloodstream infections.

Those most at risk of infection include patients with severe underlying medical conditions. In particular, those who use breathing tubes, feeding tubes, IVs or catheters are more vulnerable, as are those who are hospitalized frequently or for long periods of time.

People without those risk factors are unlikely to become colonized with C. auris or develop an infection.

Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst and clinical professor of medicine at NYU Langone, said he considers C. auris an "emerging problem of great concern."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"It is resistant to multiple antifungal drugs, and it tends to spread in hospital settings, including on equipment being used on immunocompromised and semi-immunocompromised patients, such as ventilators and catheters," he previously told Fox News Digital.

"Unfortunately, symptoms such as fever, chills and aches may be ubiquitous, and it can be mistaken for other infections."

Invasive C. auris infections have been associated with mortality rates of 30% to 72%, although most affected patients are already seriously ill. This can make it difficult to determine how often the fungus is a direct cause of death.

Candida auris can be difficult to treat because it is often resistant to antifungal medications, leading the CDC to classify the fungus as an "urgent antimicrobial-resistance threat."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

More than 90% of U.S. samples are resistant to fluconazole, a common antifungal treatment. Echinocandins, another family of antifungals, are currently the main treatment option for C. auris, although some strains are resistant to all three main classes of antifungals.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Major research" is ongoing to develop new treatments, according to Siegel.

"This is part of a much larger problem of emerging antibiotic resistance in the U.S. and around the world," the physician previously cautioned. "At the same time, sterilization and disinfection measures in hospitals can be very helpful."

Fox News Digital's Angelica Stabile contributed reporting.

Both options encrypt your internet traffic and protect your connection, but they serve different purposes. One prioritizes maximum privacy by blending your activity with thousands of other users. A shared IP is exactly what it sounds like: multiple VPN users connect through the same public IP address. When dozens, or even hundreds, of people are using the same IP at different times, it becomes much harder for websites or other observers to associate online activity with any one individual. That's one reason shared IPs are the default choice for most VPN services.

The trade-off is that shared IPs can sometimes trigger CAPTCHAs, blocked logins or extra verification if a website sees too much activity coming from the same address. That is one reason some people look for ways to fix a VPN that keeps getting blocked.

A dedicated IP is reserved exclusively for you. No one else using the VPN service shares that IP address. Because your IP remains consistent every time you connect, websites and online services recognize it as the same connection. That can make certain activities more convenient, especially if you regularly access accounts that use IP-based security checks.

For example, some businesses only allow employees to log in from approved IP addresses. Using a dedicated IP allows your company to "whitelist" this IP so that you can log in smoothly every time.

A dedicated IP can also reduce the number of verification requests you receive when signing in to banking websites, business software, or other accounts that flag unfamiliar locations. If you've ever been annoyed by a CAPTCHA (e.g., "which one of these photos is of a motorcycle?") when trying to log in from a new location, you'll appreciate the consistency of a dedicated IP address.

Some people might argue that letting your VPN provider assign you a dedicated IP inherently makes you less private. This is where your choice of VPN provider is important. A reputable VPN provider distributes IP addresses with a zero-knowledge allocation system, meaning not even the provider can trace it back to you.

With this kind of dedicated IP, you still receive the privacy and encryption benefits of a VPN; the difference is simply that your VPN IP belongs only to you.

The answer depends on how you use the internet. A shared IP is usually the better option if your main goals are privacy, anonymous browsing, and protecting your data while traveling or using public Wi-Fi. Since many people are using the same address, your online activity is more difficult to distinguish from everyone else's.

A dedicated IP makes sense if convenience is your priority. If you frequently work remotely, access company resources with IP restrictions, manage servers remotely, or want fewer login challenges from websites that recognize your connection, having your own VPN IP can save time. Neither option is inherently more secure than the other. Both encrypt your internet traffic and hide your original IP address from the websites you visit. item.title: Sherrill drops head-turning voter ID declaration in wake of registration fiasco: ‘Significant shift’
item.description: Gov. Mikie Sherrill says she would support voter ID in New Jersey, even as she blasts the federal SAVE Act that Donald Trump champions as suppression.
item.content:encoded:
New Jersey Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill says she would support a voter ID law in the Garden State — even as she slams President Donald Trump’s federal SAVE Act push as "voter suppression."

"Governor Sherrill supports the current rules requiring ID for voter registration and she is open to considering proposals to strengthen those to make sure we have the strongest, fairest elections in the nation," a spokesperson in the governor's office told Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

Sherrill’s comments hand New Jersey Republicans a new opening to press Democrats on voter ID, even as she rejects Trump’s broader federal election push under the SAVE America Act.

Sherrill's office responded to Fox News Digital on Tuesday after the Garden State Democrat told local media in July she would support a voter ID law if one were passed in New Jersey, saying she "doesn't have a problem with voter ID."

SCHUMER SAID ‘DEMOCRATS SUPPORT VOTER ID’ — THEN EVERY SENATE DEMOCRAT VOTED AGAINST GOP BILL

"I’m very opposed to the SAVE Act," Sherrill added at the time. "I do believe that is just a tool of voter suppression and an attempt to get all of the personal identifying information of New Jerseyans into the federal government systems, which I’m opposed to."

Sherrill served in the House for seven years and voted against the SAVE Act in 2025, with her office describing the measure as an "extreme voter suppression bill."

Sherrill is facing criticism after announcing last month that a Motor Vehicle Commission system error improperly registered roughly 6,600 people who had indicated they were not U.S. citizens. The state said fewer than 400 people newly registered because of the error voted, and later announced that more than 4,500 registrations were being removed while the remaining cases undergo additional review because some of those individuals may be citizens.

New Jersey Assembly Minority Leader John DiMaio told Fox News Digital Sherrill's recent comments mark a "significant shift" after years of Republicans in the Garden State advocating for voter ID.

NEW JERSEY REMOVES 6,600 PEOPLE FROM VOTER ROLLS WHO WERE ELIGIBLE TO CAST A BALLOT FOR 2024 ELECTION

"But agreeing with us publicly is the easy part," DiMaio said, adding that Democratic legislative leaders control what gets a hearing and a vote, and that Republicans have so far heard nothing from them on voter ID.

"We’ve been pushing voter ID and other election integrity reforms for years. The bills are already introduced. We’ve repeatedly called for hearings and votes. The roadblock has been Democratic legislative leadership," the Republican state leader said.

DiMaio said the Motor Vehicle System failure exposed serious weaknesses in New Jersey’s election safeguards and they still have not heard an answer of what went wrong.

Voter-ID requirements have repeatedly become major partisan fights at the state level, with Democrats and voting-rights groups arguing that some requirements can make it harder for eligible voters to cast ballots.

One of the most prominent battles erupted in Georgia in 2021. The state already required photo ID for in-person voting, but a sweeping Republican-backed election law added identification requirements for absentee voting along with other changes. The backlash went national, with MLB moving its 2021 All-Star Game out of Atlanta and some Hollywood figures threatening boycotts.

HARRIS BECOMES ACCIDENTAL SAVE ACT ‘SALESWOMAN’ AS TRUMP ATTACK SPECTACULARLY BACKFIRES

"Governor Sherrill served our country in the military and as a public servant because she believes in every citizen's right to participate in our democracy by voting. That's why she has stood firm against MAGA Republicans' voter suppression attempts and Trump’s demands for New Jersey voters’ personal identifiable information," said a spokesperson in the office of the governor.

"She has already made voting more accessible by signing the John R. Lewis Voter Empowerment Act and expanded early voting in municipal elections," the spokesperson added, referencing the law that bans voter intimidation and discrimination, expanding language assistance, and requiring extra review of election changes in places with a history of discrimination.

Trump has continued to prioritize and highlight the issue of noncitizens on voter rolls as he renewed his push for the SAVE America Act, which would require documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register for federal elections and photo identification to cast a federal ballot.

"I think they should pass Voter I.D. I think they should pass proof of citizenship—basically SAVE America Act... I think that should be something that we should absolutely get," Trump said in the Oval Office Monday.
